messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Carmen's Story

Carmen Reyes was fifty-seven years old when she came to the clinic, and she moved through the world now as though she were perpetually bracing for impact. She had been a physical therapist for thirty-two years, the kind of clinician who could read a body's compensations with her hands before a patient even spoke. That skill had made her good at her work. It had also, she believed, made her weak in the aftermath of what happened.

Seven years ago, Carmen had been visiting her sister Rosa in Puerto Rico—a trip she had taken every August for two decades. The hurricane came faster than anyone predicted. She remembered the news alerts, the sudden frantic calls from neighbors, the way the sky turned a shade of green she had never seen before. She and Rosa had sheltered in the bathroom, the only room without windows, while the house came apart around them. The sound was what stayed with her most: not the wind itself, but the sound of the roof being peeled away, a groaning metal shriek that seemed to come from the earth itself. When the water came through, it was warm and brown and full of things she could not identify. She had grabbed Rosa's hand and held it until her own fingers went numb. Her sister had survived. Carmen had survived. But something in how she inhabited her own body had not.

The triggers had assembled themselves slowly at first, then with gathering force. Water was the obvious one—she could not go near the ocean anymore, and even the sight of the bay from a distance made her stomach seize with nausea. But it was worse than simple avoidance. When she saw water, particularly still water or water that looked deep, her body would betray her with a violent wave of sickness that seemed to come from somewhere outside herself. She had stopped going to the beach entirely, which meant she had stopped seeing friends who lived near the coast. She had stopped attending her nephew's swim meets. She had begun to organize her life around the absence of water.

The name triggers were stranger to her. When she heard the name Rosa—which was common, which was everywhere—she would feel a spike of something between panic and profound sadness. It was as though her nervous system was insisting that each mention of that name was a threat, that something had gone wrong with her sister again. She had come to dread conversations, waiting for the name to appear and knowing she could not explain to people why she had suddenly become distant or quiet.

What frightened Carmen most was how much of herself she had already lost trying to manage these reactions. She had taken to deliberately leaving her body when the nausea came, a kind of dissociation that she could almost will into being. She would feel the sensation starting, and she would consciously try to float away from it, to blank out, to make herself absent. It worked for a few moments, but then she would come back to herself and realize she had lost another piece of time, another moment of her life.

She dwelled constantly on who she had been before the hurricane. She had been social, energetic, someone who loved travel and spontaneity. Now she felt trapped in a smaller and smaller space. She left her apartment less and less. Her work had suffered—she had cut back her hours, then cut back further. Her colleagues had noticed. Her supervisor had gently asked if everything was all right. Carmen had said yes, of course, while knowing that she was becoming someone unreliable, someone who cancelled plans, someone who stayed home.

The sleep had become impossible. She would lie awake for hours, listening to the sounds of the building settling, her body rigid with the certainty that something was about to happen. When she finally slept, she would wake gasping, her heart hammering, with no clear memory of a dream—just the full emotional intensity of terror, the overwhelming grief of loss, though she could not say what she had lost beyond the self she used to be.

Carmen came to the clinic on a Tuesday morning in November. She had not left her apartment for three days before that. She told the therapist that she was afraid she was disappearing entirely, and she wanted to know if that was possible, and if there was any way to come back.
